title: Security groups (stateful ENI firewall)
hook: A security group is a stateful virtual firewall attached to an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) — instance, load balancer, or VPC endpoint. It allows traffic you permit; everything else is denied, and return traffic for allowed flows is automatically permitted.

blocks.text: Security groups operate at the ENI level inside a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Rules are allow-only (no deny rules). Stateful means if you allow inbound tcp/443 from a client, return outbound packets for that flow are permitted even without an explicit outbound rule. Default: all outbound allowed, inbound denied unless added.

entries.plainDefinition: Stateful allow-list firewall bound to ENIs.
Return traffic for established allowed flows is automatically permitted.
entries.example: Inbound 443 allowed → outbound SYN-ACK permitted without explicit rule.

entries.plainDefinition: Rule referencing another SG ID instead of CIDR — dynamic membership.
Virtual network card that receives security group assignments.
entries.example: ALB, EC2, Lambda-in-VPC, Interface VPC endpoint ENIs.

blocks.text: Security groups are the primary micro-segmentation tool in AWS — tighter than Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) because they reference other SGs. Load balancer to target, bastion to database, and endpoint ENI patterns all rely on SG design. Interviewers contrast stateful SG with stateless NACL and ask about overly permissive 0.0.0.0/0 rules.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: SG is stateful ENI firewall, allow-only, supports SG-to-SG references. Default deny inbound.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Packet arrives at ENI
items.body: Security group rules on that ENI are evaluated.

items.title: Inbound allow check
items.body: Match protocol, port, and source (CIDR or SG). First match allows; no deny rules exist.

items.title: Stateful return
items.body: If inbound was allowed, related outbound response is automatically permitted.

items.title: Separate ENI evaluation
items.body: ALB ENI and target ENI each have SGs — both must permit the flow.

diagram.title: ALB to target SG chain
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  Client[Client] -->|443 allowed| ALB_SG[ALB security group]
  ALB_SG --> ALB_ENI[ALB ENI]
  ALB_ENI -->|8080 from sg-alb| APP_SG[App security group]
  APP_SG --> APP[EC2 target ENI]

snippet.label: CLI — create SG with ALB-to-app rule
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name app-sg --description "App tier" --vpc-id vpc-0abc

aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-app \
  --ip-permissions IpProtocol=tcp,FromPort=8080,ToPort=8080,UserIdGroupPairs=[{GroupId=sg-alb}]
snippet.explanation: Referencing sg-alb means any ENI in the ALB SG can reach port 8080 — no CIDR churn when targets scale.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — tiered security groups
snippet.code:
AlbSg:
  Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
  Properties:
    GroupDescription: ALB ingress
    VpcId: !Ref Vpc
    SecurityGroupIngress:
      - IpProtocol: tcp
        FromPort: 443
        ToPort: 443
        CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0

AppSg:
  Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
  Properties:
    GroupDescription: App from ALB only
    VpcId: !Ref Vpc
    SecurityGroupIngress:
      - IpProtocol: tcp
        FromPort: 8080
        ToPort: 8080
        SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref AlbSg
snippet.explanation: Three-tier pattern: edge SG open to internet on 443; app SG only from ALB SG.

snippet.label: CLI — audit overly permissive rules
snippet.explanation: Find world-open ingress before compliance scans — common interview remediation task.

snippet.label: CLI — Interface endpoint SG
snippet.explanation: Lambda SG must reach endpoint ENI SG on 443 — both sides matter for Interface VPC endpoints.

blocks.title: Network vs app auth
rows: Each HTTP request independent unless session

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Opening app SG to 0.0.0.0/0 when only ALB should reach it. Forgetting target SG must allow ALB SG on health check port. Removing all outbound rules thinking default deny outbound — default is allow all outbound.

blocks.text: Security groups are distributed — there is no central rule ordering like NACL numbers. Cross-VPC SG references require peering or shared VPC and enabled cross-reference. How to prove it in production: VPC Reachability Analyzer paths; Flow Logs REJECT on ENI implicates SG/NACL; SSM port test from bastion with known SG IDs.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Breaks patches, APIs, NTP without endpoints

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying security groups have deny rules or are stateless like NACLs. Strong answer: stateful, allow-only, ENI-bound; NACLs are stateless subnet boundary with deny support.

interviewTakeaways: Security groups are stateful, allow-only firewalls attached to ENIs.
No deny rules — implicit deny. Return traffic for allowed inbound is automatically permitted.
Reference other SGs for ALB→target and Lambda→VPC endpoint patterns.
60s: Stateful ENI firewall. Allow only. SG-to-SG for tiers. Default outbound allow. Pair with NACL for subnet deny if needed.
Follow-up: why do you need rules on both ALB and target ENIs?
commonPitfalls: Calling security groups stateless or supporting deny rules — rejected; that describes NACLs.
Strong answer: stateful allow-only at ENI; established flows return automatically.
App SG open to world on application port instead of only from ALB SG.
Interface endpoint ENI SG missing ingress from client SG — Secrets Manager timeouts.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node app listening on 8080 still needs SG allowing ALB SG — middleware auth does not replace network firewall.
ALB health checks hit target port — TypeScript app may be healthy locally but SG must allow ALB SG on that port.
